anglobe.title: The analemma on a globe: one rigid figure-8
anglobe.mini: Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and it draws a figure-8. On a globe the 8 is one rigid curve on the sky, the same for every observer: moving north or south only turns it.
anglobe.text: Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and it traces a lopsided figure-8, the analemma. Its east-west spread comes from the equation of time, ±16 minutes, and its north-south spread from the Sun's declination, ±23.44° [1]. On a globe the 8 is one rigid curve on the celestial sphere, the same for every observer at every hour: its drawn shape never changes with latitude, it only turns as you travel. The view is what a level camera aimed at the year's mean Sun would frame, at the latitude named above the text.
anglobe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: analemma photographs whose shape changes with the latitude of the camera.
anflat.title: The analemma under a flat-Earth Sun
anflat.mini: A flat-Earth Sun circling above the disc, at the height that makes the equinox noon correct for your latitude. Its figure-8 is the wrong shape, and the shape changes as you travel. No analemma photograph shows that.
anflat.text: The flat model steel-manned: its Sun circles above the disc at exactly the height that makes the equinox noon altitude correct for the latitude named above the text, the best value its one free parameter can take. Fed the same equation of time and declination as the globe [1], it still fails at mid-latitudes: solstice altitudes miss by 10° to 16° at 45° to 60° of latitude. And the flat 8 changes shape as you travel, from 65° by 16° at the equator to 29° by 11° at 60°. No analemma photograph has ever shown a shape that depends on where it was taken.
anflat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: analemma photographs from different latitudes with different shapes, matching the flat 8.
analemma.title: A year of noon Suns, two geometries
analemma.mini: The same year of Sun positions, fed through two geometries. On the globe the figure-8 is one rigid curve for everyone. Under a flat-Earth Sun, even at its best height, the 8 is misshapen and changes as you travel.
analemma.text: Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and it draws a figure-8, the analemma, from the equation of time (±16 minutes) and the declination (±23.44°) [1]. Both panels use the same inputs; only the geometry differs. On the globe, the 8 is one rigid curve on the sky, identical for every observer, which only turns as you travel. Under a flat-Earth Sun set at the height that makes the equinox noon exact for the latitude named above the text, solstice altitudes miss by 10° to 16° at mid-latitudes, and the shape of the 8 morphs from place to place. Analemma photographs from around the world all show the same figure.
analemma.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: analemma photographs whose shape depends on where they were taken.
baseline.title: The Earth's orbit as a measuring rod
baseline.mini: Jupiter's moon Io eclipses on a strict schedule. Seen from the far side of the Earth's orbit, each eclipse arrives late, by the time light takes to cross the orbit. The orbit becomes a baseline that light measures.
baseline.text: Jupiter's moon Io goes into Jupiter's shadow every 42.5 hours, a natural clock. When the Earth is on the far side of its orbit from Jupiter, each eclipse is seen late, by the time light needs to cross the extra distance; when near, early. In 1676 Rømer used this to show that light takes time to travel [1]. Run the other way, with the speed of light measured on the ground, the delay measures the orbit itself. The drawing is schematic.
baseline.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Io's eclipses arriving on the same schedule whatever the Earth's position.
romer.title: Rømer's clock, run in reverse
romer.mini: Io's eclipses drift by about 16.6 minutes as the Earth goes from the near side of its orbit to the far side. With the speed of light measured on the ground, that is the diameter of the orbit: 1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km.
romer.text: In 1676 Rømer predicted that an eclipse of Io would come 10 minutes behind the tables, and it did: light takes time to travel [1]. Now run it backwards. By 1849 Fizeau had measured the speed of light on the ground, with a toothed wheel and a mirror 8.6 km apart in Paris [2]. Fed into Io's timings, the eclipse delay swings by about 16.6 minutes between Jupiter's opposition and conjunction, and the only distance that swing can correspond to is the diameter of the Earth's orbit: 1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km [3]. Left: top view to scale in AU, the Earth lapping Jupiter every 399 days. Right: the light-travel time day by day. A flat-Earth lamp a few thousand kilometres up would give wobbles of hundredths of a second. Orbits are drawn circular and coplanar, which shifts the swing by a few percent.
romer.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Io's eclipse times drifting by hundredths of a second over the year, not by 16 minutes.
romerdata.title: The astronomical unit from 8,822 eclipses of Io
romerdata.mini: Every eclipse of Io timed from 1652 to 1983, era by era: the farther Jupiter, the later the eclipse, on one straight line. Its slope, {{rmAs}} ± {{rmDAs}} s per astronomical unit, times c measured in laboratories: {{rmAU}} ± {{rmDAU}} million km.
romerdata.text: J. H. Lieske's compilation holds {{rmIo}} timed eclipses of Io, 1652 to 1983 [1]. Fitted in six eras, each with its own clock, the shadow's geometry, Europa's 437.6-day pull on Io and one offset per observatory, the delay grows with the Earth-Jupiter distance by {{rmAs}} ± {{rmDAs}} s per astronomical unit. The orbits are angles and Jupiter's distance comes from Kepler's third law [2]: kilometres enter only through the laboratory c [3], giving {{rmAU}} ± {{rmDAU}} million km, {{rmDiff}} % from the adopted value [4]. The dots are each era's mean delay by distance; the line is one light time for all.
romerdata.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Io's clock alone fitting the eclipses as well as the light time (it leaves {{rmRmsClock}} s of scatter against {{rmRmsGlobe}} s), or a delay that does not follow the Earth-Jupiter distance.
bearing.title: The Sun's bearing, and how fast it turns
bearing.mini: The Sun's bearing, measured round the horizon from north, and the rate at which it turns. The bearing does not turn evenly, fastest around noon, but on a globe that rate follows exactly from one steady turn about the pole, 15° per hour.
bearing.text: The Sun's azimuth is its bearing measured round the horizon from north, and it can be followed hour by hour as a rate of turn. That rate is not constant: the bearing swings fastest around noon, the more so the higher the Sun passes. On a rotating globe it follows exactly from one steady motion, the Sun turning 15° per hour about the celestial pole, with the latitude and date as the only inputs. A Sun circling over a flat disc gives a different pattern of turning, which changes with the observer's distance from the centre. The drawing is schematic.
bearing.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun's bearing turning through the day in the pattern a Sun circling over a disc gives, not the globe's.
path.title: One equinox day across the whole sky
path.mini: The Sun's path on the equinox, as a whole-sky chart. On the globe it is one arc of a circle about the celestial pole, with hourly dots evenly spaced, from horizon to horizon. The flat Sun traces a lopsided loop that never reaches the horizon.
path.text: One equinox day as a whole-sky chart, zenith at the centre and horizon at the outer circle, with a dot every hour, at the latitude named above the text. The globe's path is one arc of a perfect circle about the celestial pole, the same circle long-exposure Sun and star trails show, entering and leaving at the horizon with its hourly dots evenly spaced [1]. The flat Sun traces a lopsided loop whose shape changes with latitude, dots crowded on the far side and stretched on the near side, and the loop never touches the horizon: a Sun above a flat disc never sets.
path.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a Sun whose hourly positions bunch up on the far side and that never reaches the horizon.
speed.title: How fast the Sun crosses the sky
speed.mini: The Sun's apparent angular speed through the day. Measured, it is a steady 15° per hour, as a rotating globe predicts. A flat Sun at uniform speed would swing widely; re-tuned to fix one observer, it breaks the next.
speed.text: The Sun's apparent angular speed through the day, at the latitude named above the text. Clocks, sundials and time-lapses measure a constant 15° per hour, the globe's prediction. A flat Sun circling at uniform speed would sweep this observer's sky at a rate that swings widely through the day. Re-time its track to hide that from one observer, and a second observer at 10° S, watching the same Sun at the same moments, measures a swinging rate instead. The tuning is a physical acceleration of the one shared Sun, and it must be wrong for everyone it was not tuned for. A rotating Earth keeps every sky uniform at once.
speed.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun's angular speed varying through the day by the amounts a nearby Sun requires.
daily.title: The daily motion: one sky clock for every observer
daily.mini: On a rotating globe the Sun crosses every sky along a circle about the pole at a steady 15° per hour. A Sun circling above a flat disc traces lopsided loops at uneven speeds, and no tuning fixes two observers at once.
daily.text: The Sun's daily motion for the latitude named above the text, shown two ways. On the sky chart, the globe's path is one arc of a circle about the celestial pole, from horizon to horizon, with hourly dots evenly spaced [1]; the flat Sun traces a lopsided loop that never touches the horizon. On the speed chart, the measured and predicted rate is a steady 15° per hour; the flat Sun's rate swings through the day, and re-tuning its speed for one observer breaks it for another at 10° S watching the same Sun. One rotating Earth keeps every sky's clock uniform at once.
daily.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a Sun that never sets and crosses the sky at uneven speeds.
gnomon.title: A sundial is a stick aimed at the axis
gnomon.mini: A sundial keeps time all year only if its gnomon points along the Earth's axis: tilted above the ground by exactly the latitude. Then the Sun circles it at 15° per hour, and the hour lines spread by an angle set by the latitude.
gnomon.text: A sundial keeps time all year only if its shadow-casting stick, the gnomon, is parallel to the Earth's rotation axis, pointing at the celestial pole [1]. The Sun then turns around the stick at a uniform 15° per hour whatever the season, and the hour lines can be engraved once and trusted. The price is written on every dial: the gnomon must lean above the ground by exactly the latitude, vertical at the pole, flat at the equator, 51.5° in London. That is why antique dials are cut for a stated latitude and misread when moved. The drawing is schematic.
gnomon.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a sundial that keeps time all year when moved to another latitude without re-tilting its gnomon.
dials.title: Five sundials, one Sun
dials.mini: Five sundials at 65° N, 35° N, the equator and 30° S. Each gnomon leans at its own latitude, each hour fan is different, the southern one runs anticlockwise. Yet every shadow lands on the same hour.
dials.text: Five sundials read by one Sun, at the time named above the text. Seen from the side, the gnomons lean at 65°, 35°, 0° and 30° south, each equal to its own latitude [1]. The hour fans below all differ: splayed wide at 65°, tighter at 35°, running anticlockwise on the southern dial; a horizontal dial fails outright at the equator, where the equatorial master dial takes over. Yet every shadow lands on the same hour, computed from one shadow function. Under a nearby Sun circling a flat disc, no fixed stick orientation gives season-proof hour lines, and the tilt would not follow the tilt-equals-latitude rule that dials from Egypt to China to Peru obey.
dials.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: sundials that keep time with a gnomon tilt that does not equal the latitude.
